integrated-pest-management-s1.title: Weekly pest counts on one farm

table.caption: Pest control results in two neighboring 20-hectare apple orchards over one season (invented data for practice)
cols: Orchard A: sprays on a fixed schedule

items.q: What is the main goal of integrated pest management?
options: Keep pests below damaging levels with little pesticide
Kill each pest on a farm with the strongest spray that is sold
Grow crops with no monitoring of the pests in the fields
Replace each pesticide with a stronger one each year

why.correct: IPM aims to control damage, not to wipe out every pest, while limiting pesticide use.
options: Right: control below a damaging level, with little spraying.
Total elimination with strong sprays is the approach IPM moves away from.
Monitoring is the heart of IPM.
Escalating sprays is the pesticide treadmill.

items.q: Releasing ladybugs into a greenhouse to eat aphids is an example of
options: biological control
chemical control
cultural control
a physical barrier

why.correct: Using a pest's natural enemy is biological control.
options: Right: a predator controls the pest.
No chemical is used.
Cultural control changes how and when crops are grown.
A barrier is a net, fence or row cover.

items.q: Why does IPM slow the evolution of pesticide resistance?
options: Spraying less often selects less for resistance
IPM sprays more often, so no pests survive to breed
IPM uses one pesticide each year so pests are unable to adapt
Natural enemies make the pests' genes change back

why.correct: Fewer sprayings means less selection pressure, so resistant pests gain less advantage.
options: Right: less spraying, weaker selection.
IPM sprays less, not more.
Using one product repeatedly speeds resistance; IPM rotates methods.
Predators do not change pests' genes.

items.q: Which is a drawback of IPM for a farmer?
options: It takes time, training and labor to monitor pests
It uses more pesticide than spraying on a fixed schedule
It kills more pollinators than ordinary spraying does
It speeds up the evolution of pesticide resistance

why.correct: Scouting fields, learning thresholds and managing natural enemies takes skill and time.
options: Right: knowledge and labor are the main cost.
IPM uses less pesticide.
Less spraying protects pollinators.
IPM slows resistance.

items.q: A corn farmer finds that rootworm beetles are a problem each year in fields planted with corn every year. Which IPM step targets the cause?
options: Planting soybeans in alternate years, so the larvae find no corn
Spraying the corn with insecticide each week of the season
Planting the corn a week earlier each year in the same fields
Doubling the fertilizer so that the corn plants outgrow the larvae

why.correct: Rootworm larvae feed on corn roots. In a field rotated to soybeans, larvae that hatch find no food.
options: Right: switching crops breaks the pest's life cycle.
Weekly spraying is not IPM and speeds resistance.
Same field, same corn keeps feeding the larvae.
Extra fertilizer adds runoff and does not stop the larvae.

items.q: In IPM, why is a pest count below the action threshold not treated, even though some damage occurs?
options: Treating would cost more than the damage and harm natural enemies
Pests below the threshold do no real damage to the crop plants
Pests below the threshold will die out by themselves in a few days
The law forbids treating pests until the threshold is passed

why.correct: The threshold is set where the cost of damage begins to exceed the cost (and harm) of controlling it.
options: Right: a little damage is cheaper than unneeded control.
Some damage occurs below the threshold; it is just not worth treating.
Pests below the threshold do not simply die out.
Thresholds are management choices, not laws.

items.q: A farm used 24 kg of insecticide per hectare on a fixed schedule. After switching to IPM, it uses 30% of that amount. How many kilograms per hectare does it use now?

mistakes.why: 16.8 kg is the 70% saved. The farm now uses 30% of the original.
Thirty percent is 0.30, not 30. Multiply 24 by 0.30.

items.q: A school's vegetable garden has aphids. Propose an IPM step (other than spraying a pesticide) and explain how it works.

why.correct: A step that is not a pesticide, fitted to a small garden, with how it works: release or attract ladybugs, which eat aphids, keeping the aphid population below a damaging level.

solution.label: Step
options: release ladybugs or plant flowers that attract them
spray a broad insecticide every week
stop checking the plants

why.1: The question says other than spraying a pesticide.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: eat aphids, a natural predator-prey control
poison the soil so aphids cannot lay eggs
make the plants grow faster than aphids

why.2: Ladybugs do not change plant growth.

effect.label: Result
options: the aphid population stays below a damaging level
the aphids become resistant
the ladybugs eat the vegetables

why.1: Predators do not select for pesticide resistance.

specific.model: The school could release ladybugs or plant flowers that attract them, because ladybugs eat aphids, a natural predator-prey control, so the aphid population stays below a damaging level.

items.q: In which week did the pest count pass the action threshold?
options: Week 5
Week 4
Week 10
Week 1

why.correct: Week 5 had 12 aphids per leaf, above the threshold of 10.
options: Right: 12 is above 10.
Week 4 had 8, below the threshold.
Week 10 had 9, below the threshold.
Week 1 had 2.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in the aphid count from week 5 to week 6, after the targeted control, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the week 5 count of 12.
Subtract old from new: (6 - 12). The count fell, so the change is negative.
-6 aphids per leaf is the change. Divide by 12 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from week 6 back to week 5. Start from week 5.

items.q: A farm on a fixed schedule sprays every two weeks. How many sprayings would it make in these 10 weeks, compared with the IPM farm's one?
options: 5 sprayings, compared with 1
10 sprayings, compared with 1
2 sprayings, compared with 1
1 spraying, the same as IPM

why.correct: Every two weeks over 10 weeks is $\frac{10}{2} = 5$ sprayings; IPM sprayed once, in week 5.
options: That would be weekly spraying.
Every two weeks gives more than 2 in 10 weeks.
The fixed schedule sprays regardless of counts.

items.q: In weeks 7 to 10 the count rose again from 4 to 9. What should the IPM farmer do?
options: Keep monitoring and act again if the count passes 10
Spray right away because the count is rising
Stop monitoring because the count is below 10
Release a new pesticide each week to stop the rise

why.correct: IPM acts on the threshold, not on any rise; at 9 the count is still below 10.
options: Right: watch and wait until the threshold.
A rise below the threshold does not call for spraying.
Monitoring continues all season.
Weekly pesticides are the opposite of IPM.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in insecticide used per hectare from orchard A to orchard B, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, orchard A's 18 kg per ha.
That is B as a percent of A (27.8%). Percent change subtracts first: (5 - 18) / 18 × 100.
-13 kg per ha is the change. Divide by 18 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from B to A. Start from orchard A.

items.q: How much money does orchard B save on pest control across its whole 20 hectares, compared with orchard A?

mistakes.why: 400 dollars is the saving per hectare. Multiply by the 20 hectares.
That is orchard B's total cost. The saving is the difference times 20 ha.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: IPM cut spraying and cost, with slightly more damage
IPM raised damaged apples sharply while costing more than spraying
Fixed spraying protected the predatory mites better than IPM did
IPM and fixed spraying used about the same amount of insecticide

why.correct: B sprayed 4 times instead of 12, used 5 kg instead of 18, cost 400 dollars less per ha; damage was 4% against 3%.
options: Right: much less spraying and cost, slightly more damage.
Damage rose by one percentage point, and IPM cost less.
Predatory mites were far higher under IPM (2.5 against 0.2).
5 and 18 kg per ha are far apart.

items.q: Why might orchard B need fewer sprayings in future seasons as well?
options: Its predatory mites survive and eat the pest mites
Its pests have become resistant, so spraying them is no longer needed
Its apples are damaged more, so pests have less to eat next year
Its insecticide stays on the trees for many seasons after spraying

why.correct: Protecting natural enemies builds lasting biological control.
options: Right: surviving predators keep controlling pests.
Resistance would make spraying fail, not unnecessary.
More damage does not starve the pests.
Long-lasting residues are not the IPM benefit.

items.q: Put the steps of an IPM program in a sensible order.
options: Identify the pest and learn its life cycle
Monitor pest numbers regularly
Compare counts with the action threshold
Use biological, physical or cultural controls first
Use a targeted pesticide only if needed, then keep monitoring

why.correct: Know the pest, watch it, decide by threshold, start with the least harmful tools, and spray only as a last resort.
